notes: Commercial Court summary judgment on discretionary bonus and restitution claims; Cooke J's reasoning is detailed.

enrichment.short_title: Taylor v Motability: summary judgment on RVI bonus and restitution claims
key_facts: Finance Director Taylor negotiated a highly successful £80m-plus RVI insurance recovery for Motability but was dismissed after receiving the maximum 50% special project bonus.

His contract provided discretionary bonuses capped at 50% of salary after a February 2003 remuneration committee decision; he claimed bad faith, a proportionate bonus of 0.5% of recovery, and restitutionary relief.
Motability applied under CPR 24.2 to strike out or obtain summary judgment on bad faith, excess bonus and restitution pleas.
The parties disputed whether CEO Lester had induced an expectation of a bonus linked to the RVI outcome.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interlocutory application in the Commercial Court for summary judgment and striking out parts of re-amended particulars and reply.
enrichment.outcome: Motability's applications succeeded; bad faith and restitution claims were struck out or summarily dismissed and claims above the 50% special bonus cap had no real prospect of success.
enrichment.ratio: Where an employee has fully performed under an employment contract and seeks bonus damages, contractual remedies govern and there is no room for concurrent restitution; a discretionary bonus decision is reviewed on rationality under Horkulak v Cantor Fitzgerald, not on what a reasonable employer would pay.
legal_issues: Whether bad faith in awarding the maximum special bonus was properly pleaded
Whether a claim exceeding the contractual bonus cap could be irrational
Whether restitution lay outside the employment contract after wrongful dismissal
Whether failure to communicate bonus caps earlier breached trust and confidence
linked_authorities: Horkulak v Cantor Fitzgerald International [2004] EWCA Civ 1287
Johnson v Agnew [1980] AC 367
Henderson v Merrett Syndicates Ltd [1995] 2 AC 145

confidence.notes: Interlocutory dispositions and governing House of Lords restitution principles are clearly stated.

notes: Long Commercial Court judgment on s44(2)(e) interim injunction restraining charter-party withdrawal pending arbitration.

enrichment.short_title: LauritzenCool v Lady Navigation: interim injunction under Arbitration Act 1996 s44
key_facts: LauritzenCool chartered two modern reefer vessels Lady Racisce and Lady Korcula from Lady Navigation under ten-year Cooltime 95 pool charters running to 2010.
After a change of ownership the owners sought to withdraw the vessels from Lauritzen's proprietary reefer pool and threatened EC competition complaints.
Lauritzen commenced withdrawal arbitration and sought a s44 interim injunction preventing inconsistent employment of the vessels pending final award.
Lord Millett had found Lauritzen owed fiduciary duties to pool owners in a separate duties arbitration.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interim injunction application under section 44(2)(e) of the 1996 Act pending arbitration on validity of charters and withdrawal rights.
enrichment.outcome: Interim injunction granted in terms restraining employment of the vessels inconsistently with the charters until final arbitration award.
enrichment.ratio: Negative injunctions restraining use of a vessel outside a time charter are not impermissible decrees of specific performance following Scaptrade; damages were inadequate given the vessels' unique value to the charterer's pool and NOBSK commitments.
legal_issues: Whether s44 injunctions against charter-party breach amount to specific performance
Whether fiduciary pool charters resemble personal services contracts
Adequacy of damages where modern reefer tonnage would be lost to competitors
Balance of convenience pending EC and arbitral proceedings
linked_authorities: Scaptrade v Benedetti [1983] 2 AC 694
De Mattos v Gibson (1859) 4 DeG & J 276
Lord Strathcona Steamship Co Ltd v Dominion Coal Co [1926] AC 108

confidence.notes: Interlocutory relief granted with extensive historical analysis; merits of withdrawal remain for arbitration.

notes: Chancery appeal on mandatory stay under section 9 where audit-right dispute was held arbitrable.

enrichment.short_title: Rolling Stones v Decca: stay of audit claim under section 9 Arbitration Act
key_facts: Three Rolling Stones members sued Decca for refusing documents needed to audit royalties under 1976 agreements with Leopold Joseph.
The agreements contained a Scott v Avery arbitration clause limiting arbitral remedies to payment of sums awarded.
Claimants argued clause 6 conferred a substantive audit right not compensable in damages and therefore outside arbitration.
Decca appealed against refusal of a mandatory stay under section 9.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a master's refusal to stay High Court proceedings under section 9 of the 1996 Act.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; proceedings stayed because breach of the audit clause was arbitrable and damages/account would require the same disclosure.
enrichment.ratio: A wide arbitration clause and pecuniary-remedy proviso do not deprive an audit clause of substance where the measure of damages for non-performance is what an audit would have revealed, so the arbitrator must order equivalent document production.
legal_issues: Whether a breach of an audit clause falls within a Scott v Avery arbitration agreement
Whether limiting remedies to money awards is repugnant to a substantive audit right
Construction of 'in connection with' in the arbitration clause
Mandatory nature of section 9 stay where no exceptions apply
linked_authorities: Ashville Investments Ltd v Elmer Contractors Ltd [1989] QB 488
Scott v Avery (1856) 5 HLC 811

confidence.notes: Stay outcome and contractual construction are clearly reasoned on agreed mandatory-stay principles.

notes: Massive spares quantum judgment after admitted conversion; final principal and interest figures agreed by experts.

enrichment.short_title: Kuwait Airways v Iraqi Airways: quantum for converted aircraft spares
key_facts: Following Iraq's 1990 invasion of Kuwait, Iraqi Airways admitted converting Kuwait Airways aircraft spare parts stored at Kuwait International Airport from 9 August 1990.
The spares action was part of long-running litigation over aircraft and parts seized during the invasion.
IAC disputed quantum based on MSCS inventory data, remaindered/recovered/lost spares categories, betterment, bulk discounts and user damages.
An interim payment of about US$148.5m had already been ordered before final judgment.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial on quantum in the Commercial Court after admitted liability for conversion of spare parts.
enrichment.outcome: Judgment for KAC with final principal of US$161,951,961 plus interest, within an agreed cap of US$365,825,649 including interest.
enrichment.ratio: Where a converter uses large quantities of spare parts over long periods, just compensation may combine percentage-of-list-price value awards, repair and PIP costs, and monthly user-style compensation calibrated to avoid double recovery rather than a conventional single-measure conversion award.
legal_issues: Reliability of KAC remaindered and recovered inventory data
Appropriate MLP percentages for remaindered, recovered and lost spares
Entitlement to user damages for periods of wrongful use
Betterment, bulk discount and simulator spares consent-order issues
linked_authorities: Kuwait Airways Corp v Iraqi Airways Co [2002] UKHL 19
Livingstone v Rawyards Coal Co (1880) 5 App Cas 25

confidence.notes: Final figures were agreed by party experts though the underlying fact-finding is exceptionally complex.

notes: TCC jurisdiction challenge on Italian forum clause versus Brussels Regulation Article 6(2) Part 20 claim.

enrichment.short_title: British Sugar v Babbini: Article 23 jurisdiction over Italian forum clause
key_facts: British Sugar bought a pulp press from Italian supplier Babbini; the gearbox was supplied under a separate contract between Babbini and BF Engineering governed by Italian law.
The gearbox contract contained an exclusive Forli jurisdiction clause in standard Italian purchase conditions.
After British Sugar settled its main claim, Babbini pursued BF in English Part 20 proceedings relying on Article 6(2).
BF applied for a declaration that the English court had no jurisdiction and to set aside service.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Technology and Construction Court application to decline jurisdiction over Part 20 claim against Italian domiciled supplier.
enrichment.outcome: BF succeeded; the Forli clause fell within Article 23 and took precedence over Article 6(2), and after main action settlement Part 20 proceedings could not continue in England.
enrichment.ratio: An exclusive Italian competenza clause selecting the courts of Forli is an Article 23 agreement conferring jurisdiction on a Member State court for all disputes, including international ones, and prevails over a later Article 6(2) third-party claim once the main action has ended.
legal_issues: Whether an Italian competenza clause is confined to internal territorial allocation or governs international jurisdiction
Need for an international element under the Judgments Regulation
Interaction of Articles 23 and 6(2)
Whether Part 20 proceedings remained appropriate after settlement
linked_authorities: Hough v P & O Containers Ltd [1999] QB 834
Powell Duffryn Plc v Petereit [1992] ECR I-1745
Provimi Ltd v Aventis Animal Nutrition SA [2003] EWHC 961 (Comm)

notes: CCRC reference allowing very historic receiving conviction appeal on fresh Jamieson identification evidence.

enrichment.short_title: R v Quinn: CCRC reference quashing 1957 receiving conviction
key_facts: John Quinn was convicted in 1957 of receiving stolen brass and lead after acquittal on store-breaking, based mainly on accomplice Harry Dixon's evidence.
Jamieson and Miller were convicted separately in the magistrates' court of receiving the same property from Dixon.
In 2003 Jamieson stated Quinn was not the man with Dixon when lead was sold, differing in size from the actual seller.
The CCRC referred the case as fresh evidence despite loss of trial transcripts and original appeal refusal in 1957.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal criminal division hearing treated as appeal by CCRC reference under section 9 of the 1995 Act.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; Jamieson's fresh evidence admitted under section 23 and the 1957 receiving conviction quashed.
enrichment.ratio: Even where reasonable explanation for not calling a witness at trial is not clearly shown, section 23 permits admission of fresh credible evidence in exceptional historic cases where it materially undermines the prosecution case and would render the conviction unsafe.
legal_issues: Whether Jamieson's evidence was fresh and admissible under section 23
Whether there was a reasonable explanation for not calling Jamieson at trial
Effect of separate trials of co-receivers on fairness
Safety of a conviction depending solely on Dixon's evidence
linked_authorities: R v Ditch (1969) 53 Cr App R 627
Beresford 56 Cr App R 146

confidence.notes: Outcome turns on exceptional facts and lost records; court discouraged routine referral of historic cases.

notes: Formula One corporate governance appeal on Article 22 exclusive jurisdiction and Lugano stay issues.

enrichment.short_title: Speed Investments v Formula One: Article 22 company seat jurisdiction
key_facts: Speed Investments and Bambino disputed whether Argand directors were validly appointed to the board of English company Formula One Holdings.
The SLEC Shareholders Agreement contained an exclusive Geneva jurisdiction clause potentially displaced by Brussels/Lugano rules.
English proceedings sought declarations on board composition and register rectification; Bambino commenced parallel Geneva proceedings.
Swiss-domiciled Argands argued the English court should stay under Lugano Article 21 as Geneva was first seised.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Lewison J on whether English courts had exclusive jurisdiction and should stay proceedings against Swiss defendants.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; Article 22(2) gave exclusive jurisdiction to English courts and Article 21 did not require a stay where the second court had exclusive jurisdiction.
enrichment.ratio: Proceedings whose subject matter is the composition of a company's board fall within Article 22(2) regardless of whether resolution requires construction of a shareholders' agreement, and exclusive jurisdiction under Article 16/22 displaces mandatory lis pendens rules in Article 21.
legal_issues: Whether director appointment disputes are proceedings on validity of company organs
Restrictive versus purposive construction of Article 22
Whether Lugano Article 21 applies where second court has Article 16 exclusive jurisdiction
Which court was first seised
linked_authorities: Grupo Torras v Al-Sabah [1996] 1 LlR 7
Ashurst v Pollard [2001] Ch 595
Overseas Union Insurance v New Hampshire [1992] 1 QB 434

confidence.notes: Jurisdictional holdings are clearly reasoned though some lis pendens points were left open.

notes: Planning appeal restoring permission refusal where inspector misapplied PPG8 health guidance on mobile masts near schools.

enrichment.short_title: T-Mobile v SoS: PPG8 and health concerns at Harrogate phone mast
key_facts: Harrogate Borough Council refused planning permission for extending a shared mobile phone mast near several schools.
The Secretary of State's inspector dismissed the operators' appeal on health grounds despite ICNIRP compliance and self-certification.
PPG8 stated that where ICNIRP guidelines are met planning authorities should not need to consider further health aspects.
Operators had corresponded with schools providing technical reassurance about emissions and beam intensity.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal under section 288 against quashing of inspector's decision refusing planning permission for telecommunications equipment.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; inspector's decision was quashed because he misconstrued PPG8 and failed adequately to explain refusing permission once ICNIRP compliance was established.
enrichment.ratio: PPG8 paragraph 98 is planning policy that ICNIRP-compliant mast proposals should not be refused on perceived health grounds unless exceptionally justified; perceived concern is not a substitute for departing from that policy without reasons.
legal_issues: Construction of PPG8 paragraphs 97 and 98 on health in planning decisions
Whether Stewart Report beam-of-greatest-intensity concerns override ICNIRP compliance
Adequacy of inspector's reasons on reassurance to schools
Distinction between actual and perceived health risk in planning
linked_authorities: Gransden v Secretary of State for the Environment [1986] JPL 519

confidence.notes: Policy construction and procedural defect findings are explicit in the Court of Appeal judgment.

notes: Housing benefit appeal holding registered legal owner definition excludes beneficial-only trustees.

enrichment.short_title: Burton v New Forest: housing benefit and registered owner definition

statutes_considered.title: Social Security Contributions and Benefits Act 1992

key_facts: Disabled barrister Stephen Burton occupied 12 Carvers Lane and claimed housing benefit paying rent to the Nay Housing Care Trust.
He had been registered as sole proprietor at the Land Registry until April 2002 despite holding property on trust without beneficial interest.
The council refused benefit because regulation 10(2)(c) excludes payments by an owner and he remained registered owner when he applied in November 2001.
A tribunal allowed his appeal distinguishing legal and beneficial ownership, but the Commissioner restored the refusal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from a Social Security Commissioner's decision on meaning of 'owner' in housing benefit regulations.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; Burton was an owner within regulation 2(1) while registered with title absolute and therefore disqualified from housing benefit for payments to the trust.
enrichment.ratio: Under regulation 2(1) 'owner' means the person entitled to dispose of the fee simple, which includes a registered proprietor able to convey free of trust interests under section 20(1) LRA 1925, not merely a beneficial owner or trustee without register entry.
legal_issues: Whether owner in regulation 2(1) means beneficial or registered legal owner
Effect of trust deed where Land Registry still showed sole proprietorship
Interaction of regulations 7, 10(2)(c) and 2(1)
Whether rent liability to trust avoided section 130(2)(b) mortgage exclusion
linked_authorities: Charles Fairbank v Lambeth Magistrates Court [2002] EWHC 785 (Admin)
R v Sheffield Housing Benefits Review Board ex parte Smith (1995) 28 HLR 36

notes: Administrative Court appeal reversing absurd no-case submission on labelled alcohol product evidence.

enrichment.short_title: Sunderland v Dawson: underage alcohol sale and section 24 evidence
key_facts: Trading Standards used a 15-year-old test purchaser to buy Lambrini labelled as 7.5% alcohol from a village shop licensee.
The licensee admitted the sale and said she relied on appearance rather than asking for ID.
Defence counsel submitted no case to answer because no certificate of analysis proved the bottle contained alcohol.
Magistrates upheld the submission without prosecution response and the council appealed by case stated.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Administrative Court appeal by case stated from magistrates' acceptance of submission of no case to answer.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; magistrates erred in law and the matter was remitted, with costs orders against the shop proprietor including legal aid costs.
enrichment.ratio: A labelled commercial product's description is admissible under section 24 as evidence of its contents without chemical analysis unless there is reason to doubt it, following DEFRA v Atkinson; requiring analysis of routine retail alcohol would be absurd.
legal_issues: Admissibility of product labelling under section 24 Criminal Justice Act 1988
Whether alcohol content must be proved by analysis in underage sale prosecutions
Propriety of no-case submission and magistrates' legal advice
Costs consequences on case stated appeal
linked_authorities: Department for the Environment, Food and Rural Affairs v Atkinson [2002] EWHC 2028 (Admin)
Foxley [1995] 2 Cr App R 523
